name: Indonesian
variety: Standard Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia) as spoken in Jakarta and Java; the regional first language of the speaker (Javanese, Sundanese, Batak and others) affects vowel quality and prosody
sources: Soderberg, Craig D. & Olson, Kenneth S. (2008). Indonesian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 38(2), 209-213.
Lapoliwa, Hans (1981). A Generative Approach to the Phonology of Bahasa Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-34. Canberra: Australian National University.
van Zanten, Ellen (1989). The Indonesian Vowels: Acoustic and Perceptual Explorations. PhD dissertation, Leiden University.

van Zanten, Ellen & van Heuven, Vincent J. (1984). The Indonesian vowels as pronounced and perceived by Toba Batak, Sundanese and Javanese speakers. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 140, 497-521.

van Zanten, Ellen, Goedemans, Rob & Pacilly, Jos (2003). The status of word stress in Indonesian. In J. van de Weijer, V. J. van Heuven & H. van der Hulst (eds.), The Phonological Spectrum, vol. 2, 151-175. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
van Zanten, Ellen & Goedemans, Rob (2009). Prominence in Indonesian: stress, phrases, and boundaries. Wacana 11(2).
van Heuven, Vincent J. & van Zanten, Ellen (eds.) (2007). Prosody in Indonesian Languages. Utrecht: LOT.
Halim, Amran (1981). Intonation in Relation to Syntax in Indonesian. Pacific Linguistics D-36. Canberra: Australian National University.
Cohn, Abigail C. (1989). Stress in Indonesian and bracketing paradoxes. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 7, 167-216.
Adisasmito-Smith, Niken (1999). Influence of Javanese vowel patterning on Indonesian: an acoustic investigation. Proceedings of the 14th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, San Francisco.
Sneddon, James Neil (1996). Indonesian: A Comprehensive Grammar. London: Routledge.
contrasts: six vowels including schwa; the spelling writes both /e/ and /ə/ as e
voiced versus voiceless stops and affricates at four places
four nasals m n ɲ ŋ
no vowel or consonant length, no tone
f, z, ʃ, x occur only in loanwords
allophony: voiceless stops are unaspirated, and unreleased at the end of a syllable
syllable-final /k/ is a glottal stop [ʔ] in native words (tidak, becak); it stays [k] in some loans (fakta) and in some regional accents
/t/ is dental for many speakers while /d/ is alveolar
voiced stops may be slightly breathy; they do not occur word-finally in native words and are devoiced there in loans (murid with final [t])

/i e o u/ are lowered to [ɪ ɛ ɔ ʊ] in a final closed syllable, and in the syllable before it when both vowels agree in height; the strength of the effect depends on the regional background of the speaker
/r/ is a trill, sometimes a tap between vowels
a glottal stop separates a prefix ending in a vowel from a stem beginning with one (seorang, keenam), like vowels across a morpheme boundary (keadaan), and the vowels of some Arabic loans (maaf)
/x/ is giving way to /k/ or /h/; f, z, ʃ are replaced by p, dʒ or s, s in colloquial speech; the letter v is pronounced [f]
/h/ between unlike vowels and at the end of a word is dropped in some regional accents
schwa is short and is often dropped between a consonant and a following liquid or in prefixes
syllable_structure: (C)V(C); consonant clusters in onsets only in loanwords
phonotactics: codas are limited to p t k (as [ʔ]) m n ŋ s h r l in native words; palatals and voiced stops do not close a syllable
the diphthongs ai, au, oi occur only at the end of a root in an open syllable; in closed syllables the same letters are two syllables (la.ut, ba.ik, da.un)
a nasal before a stop is homorganic inside a root

stress.type: weak and non-contrastive; prominence belongs to the phrase rather than the word
stress.rule: Traditional descriptions put stress on the penultimate syllable, moving it to the final syllable when the penultimate vowel is schwa; experimental work finds no communicatively relevant word stress and places a prominence-lending pitch movement near the end of the phrase.
stress.cues: pitch movement on the last two syllables of the phrase; duration and intensity differences between syllables are small

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: only schwa is short and may be dropped; full vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: Word-final high vowels in open syllables averaged 94 to 105 ms against 58 to 59 ms in final closed syllables (Adisasmito-Smith 1999, six speakers, words in a carrier phrase). I know of no published nPVI for Indonesian; see the Malay profile for Malay values.

length.notes: No length contrasts. Double vowel letters are two syllables, often with a glottal stop between them (maaf, saat).

intonation.declarative: the final phrase carries a rise and fall over its last two syllables and ends low; earlier phrases (the topic) end high
intonation.yes_no_question: a statement becomes a question by a final rise; with the question word apakah or the clitic -kah the final rise is optional
intonation.wh_question: the question word carries a pitch peak; the utterance usually ends with a fall
intonation.continuation: rise on the last syllable of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: rise and fall aligned with the last two syllables of a phrase, not with a lexically stressed syllable
intonation.notes: After Halim (1981) and the studies in van Heuven & van Zanten (2007). The shape and alignment of the movements differ with the regional background of the speaker.

phonation: slightly breathy voiced stops for some speakers
unreleased final stops; glottal stop for final k

problems: the letter e is guessed from stress: a stressed e becomes [ɛ] and an unstressed one [ə], so words with schwa in the penultimate syllable are wrong (besar, kecil, keras, emas come out with stressed [ɛ]); only a few words are corrected in the word list
final k is a released [k] (tidak, anak, bapak); the glottal stop appears only in a few listed words
ai and au are made diphthongs in closed syllables too, where the standard has two syllables (laut, baik, daun come out as one syllable)
fixed penultimate stress with clearly longer and louder stressed vowels, where the literature finds weak or no word stress and a phrase-final pitch movement
no lowering of high and mid vowels in final closed syllables
final stops are released; sy is [ç] rather than [ʃ]; v is voiced [v]
good: the prefixes be-, ke-, me-, pe-, se-, ter- get schwa by rule
a short break is inserted between identical vowels (maaf, saat), close to the glottal stop of the standard
ng, ny, kh are read as ŋ, ɲ, x

notes: van Zanten & van Heuven (1984) and van Zanten (1989) give formant tables for the six vowels; I could not read the numbers reliably and therefore give no formant block.
